claims.text: Rapid quenching produces a homogeneous NiFeCoCr-based solid solution.
Approximately 700°C is below the order-disorder transition for the proposed NiFeCoCr-based alloy.
Subcritical annealing promotes nanoscale compositional fluctuations relative to a rapidly quenched baseline.
Subcritical annealing produces localized strain fields in the alloy.
Annealing-induced compositional fluctuations and strain fields act as magnetic domain-wall pinning sites.
The proposed microstructural inhomogeneities impede smooth domain-wall motion.
Greater domain-wall pinning requires a larger external field to reverse magnetization and therefore raises coercivity.
The annealed alloy will have a measurably higher coercive field than the rapidly quenched baseline.
The rapidly quenched baseline has a relatively uniform distribution of exchange-coupling energies and consequently lower coercivity.
The coercivity increase should hold for bulk samples measured at room temperature or another defined operating temperature in the absence of significant external stress.
The beneficial effect requires annealing parameters that create pinning sites without excessive grain growth or full phase separation.
Extreme annealing may eliminate beneficial inhomogeneities or induce unwanted phases.
Heat treatment can make NiFeCoCr-based alloys more magnetically homogeneous by narrowing the distribution of exchange energies.
The treatment response reflects a balance between enhanced pinning and over-homogenization.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says that only an optimized but presently unknown annealing window should work, yet it treats a null result at the single example condition of 700°C for 2 hours as falsification. Such a null result could instead be attributed to testing outside the asserted optimum.
